h1:
Lamphun Cafe & Rice Field Plan
2 Slow Days by the Paddies
intro: Lamphun is a small town most people just drive through on the way to Chiang Mai, but if you love coffee and green rice fields, it's the kind of place worth staying a night for. A lot of the cafes here sit right in the middle of working paddies, with distant mountains in view and barely a crowd. We've put together a 2-day plan for cruising the rice-field cafes, stopping at old temples, and wandering a quiet town with nowhere to be.

blocks.html: Lamphun sits only about 30 km from Chiang Mai, roughly an hour's drive, so plenty of people tack it on as an extension of a Chiang Mai trip. What makes Lamphun worth an overnight is the wave of rice-field cafes that have popped up around the Makhuea Chae, Pa Sang and Ban Hong areas. Coffee still runs from the tens to low hundreds of baht, but the view is green paddies and mountains. This plan is built for a slow-life two days and one night: sit for a long time, take photos, and eat local food along the way.

blocks.title: When are the fields greenest
blocks.html: Lamphun's rice fields turn deep green from the rainy season into early winter, roughly July to November. The golden harvest fields come later, in late November to December. Come in the rainy season if you want the lushest green; come in winter if you'd rather have cool breezes and easy cafe afternoons.

blocks.text: Day 1 — In-town paddy cafes + old temples

blocks.html: Start day one in central Lamphun, walk a temple or two to soak up the old-town feel, then drift out to the Makhuea Chae area where you can settle into a rice-field cafe right through to the evening.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Old town + Makhuea Chae paddy cafes

items.activity: Early breakfast: khao soi or khanom jeen nam ngiao in town
items.note: Local shops around Nong Dok market and the town center open early, with plates starting at 35–60 THB. Eat before noon since several places sell out fast.

items.activity: Pay respects at Wat Phra That Hariphunchai
items.note: The golden chedi has been Lamphun's landmark for over a thousand years, right in the town center. It's easy to walk around and photograph the gateways and the chedi. Free entry, donate as you wish.

items.activity: Stroll the old moat and the Queen Chamthewi Monument
items.note: Lamphun town is tiny, so you can easily walk the old moat. Pop into shops selling woven textiles and dried longan along the way.

items.activity: Head to Makhuea Chae for a long sit at a paddy cafe
items.note: It's about 15–20 minutes from town out toward Makhuea Chae, the area with the highest concentration of rice-field cafes in Lamphun.

items.activity: Relax at Sip Whisper, a wooden cafe by the paddies
items.note: A homey-style cafe set in the fields of Makhuea Chae, looking out over green paddies and distant mountains. Open daily except Wednesday, roughly 9am to evening, with coffee, cake and one-plate meals. Drinks start around 55–75 THB.

items.activity: Move to another cafe nearby, or shoot the surrounding fields
items.note: Around Makhuea Chae you'll find Flip n' Flow Home Cafe and Bakehouse (closed Wednesday), a warm-toned home bakery cafe that's good for carrying on into the afternoon.

items.activity: Back into town for lodging and dinner
items.note: Lamphun goes quiet at night, but northern restaurants and made-to-order shops in town stay open. A small evening market gives you that calm small-town feel.

blocks.title: Getting around
blocks.html: Lamphun doesn't have much public transport in town, and the rice-field cafes are spread far apart. It's best to rent a car or motorbike from Chiang Mai and drive over, which is far smoother than relying on hired rides.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Field-view cafes around Pa Sang and Ban Hong

blocks.html: Day two heads to the south of the province toward Pa Sang and Ban Hong. This zone is old cotton-weaving towns and fruit orchards, with paddy-view and mountain-view cafes that most people haven't gotten around to. Coffee tends to be noticeably cheaper than in the tourist-town cafes.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Pa Sang–Ban Hong: field and mountain views

items.activity: Check out, then drive down to Pa Sang
items.note: It's about 20 minutes from Lamphun town to Pa Sang district, with the road passing rice fields and longan orchards in stretches. Easy to stop for roadside photos along the way.

items.activity: Walk old-town Pa Sang for the wooden houses and cotton shops
items.note: Pa Sang is a long-standing hand-woven cotton district with old wooden homes to photograph. A nice warm-up before the cafes.

items.activity: Sip coffee over the fields at The Lamp Lamphun Farm Café
items.note: A farm cafe in Pa Sang with a garden, a pond and animals the kids love. The wide country-garden setting is good for a long sit, and works for a late breakfast too.
Try khanom jeen nam ngiao or a long-running noodle shop in Pa Sang market, at local prices of 40–60 THB a plate.

items.activity: On to View Doi, a cafe in a date-palm grove
items.note: Sitting on the Ban Hong–Wiang Nong Long boundary, it's a country-garden cafe set among date palms with plenty of photo corners. Open and fresh, good for anyone who loves garden and mountain views.

items.activity: Wrap up at Phufin Coffee with Pa Sang field views
items.note: The owner's own line is "cheap coffee, million-baht views." There are trees, flowers and selfie corners, friendly prices, and it's an easy photo stop before heading back.

items.activity: Grab dried longan and cotton souvenirs, then head home
items.note: If you're returning to Chiang Mai it's about an hour's drive. If you're continuing on, Pa Sang is close to the routes up toward Lampang and Tak.

blocks.text: Lamphun's talked-about paddy and field-view cafes

blocks.html: If the timing doesn't fit the plan, just pick the spots you want from this list. All of them are open and have steady reviews, ordered by how well they suit a rice-field, slow-life kind of trip.

items.name: Sip Whisper
items.blurb: A homey wooden cafe set in the paddies of Makhuea Chae. The draw is the green fields and distant mountains, quiet and relaxed, made for sitting a whole afternoon.

items.name: The Lamp Lamphun Farm Café
items.blurb: A farm cafe in Pa Sang with a garden, a pond and animals, good for families. Have a late breakfast and let the kids roam the garden.

items.name: View Doi
items.blurb: A country-garden cafe set in a date-palm grove on the Ban Hong–Wiang Nong Long boundary. Open and fresh with lots of photo corners, and still off most people's radar.
items.meta: Ban Hong/Wiang Nong Long · garden cafe

items.name: Phufin Coffee
items.blurb: A field-view cafe in Pa Sang, with the owner's own slogan of "cheap coffee, million-baht views." Trees, flowers, a mock waterfall and selfie corners.
items.price: Coffee in the tens of baht

items.name: Baan Him Fai
items.blurb: A small cafe in Pa Sang with paddy views and a calm feel. Good for sitting quietly solo or as a pair, never crowded.

items.name: Suksud Gelato Coffee & Bakery
items.blurb: A new homey, Japanese-style cafe in Pa Sang, known for its gelato and homemade ice cream, with warm wooden-house photo corners.

items.name: Route 116 Coffee Bar Pasang
items.blurb: A retro-style cafe in Pa Sang done up in wood and orange brick, an easy stop for coffee and a pastry along the way.

items.name: Flip n' Flow Home Cafe and Bakehouse
items.blurb: A warm-toned home bakery cafe in Makhuea Chae, good for carrying on into the afternoon after the paddy-side cafes. Fresh-baked goods.

blocks.title: Always check before you go
blocks.html: Many of the rice-field cafes are small owner-run spots, and their days off and opening hours shift with the season and the weather. Before driving out far, it's worth checking their Facebook page or calling ahead so you don't make the trip for nothing.

blocks.text: What else to stop for along the way

items.name: Nong Chang Khuen
items.blurb: A longan-orchard and rice-field area north of town, good for cruising around and photographing fields and fruit orchards.

items.name: Nong Ngueak Weaving Village
items.blurb: A hand-woven cotton village in Pa Sang where you can watch the looms and buy cotton textiles as souvenirs.

items.name: Wat Chamthewi (Ku Kut)
items.blurb: An old stepped, square chedi in the town center, a rare piece of Hariphunchai architecture worth stopping for before you leave town.

blocks.text: Rough budget per person, 2 days 1 night

items: Lodging in Lamphun town — guesthouse / small hotel, about 500–1,200 THB/night
4–5 cafes — drinks plus snacks, roughly 400–700 THB total
Fuel / car rental — budget around 400–800 THB if coming from Chiang Mai
Rough total — about 1,600–3,000 THB/person, depending on lodging and food

faq.q: Which areas have Lamphun's paddy-side cafes?
faq.a: They cluster in three main areas: Makhuea Chae near town (such as Sip Whisper and Flip n' Flow), Pa Sang district (The Lamp Lamphun, Phufin, Baan Him Fai, Route 116, Suksud), and the Ban Hong–Wiang Nong Long side (View Doi). All are about 15–30 minutes' drive from Lamphun town.

faq.q: When's the best time to visit Lamphun for the rice-field cafes?
faq.a: The paddies are deep green from the rainy season into early winter, roughly July to November. Winter brings just-right cool weather for easy cafe sitting, and if you want to see the golden harvest fields, come in late November to December.

faq.q: Can I do this plan without a private vehicle?
faq.a: It's fairly tough, since the rice-field cafes are far apart and public transport in Lamphun is scarce. The easiest way is to rent a car or motorbike in Chiang Mai and drive down, which takes only about an hour from Chiang Mai.

faq.q: How much does a 2-day Lamphun cafe trip cost?
faq.a: About 1,600–3,000 THB per person for 2 days and 1 night, including a guesthouse, 4–5 cafes, local meals and fuel. Lamphun is a town you can travel on a modest budget.

faq.q: Can I visit Lamphun and Chiang Mai on the same trip?
faq.a: Easily. Lamphun is only about 30 km from Chiang Mai, so plenty of people use it as a one-day add-on from Chiang Mai, or stay a night to do the rice-field cafe circuit without rushing.
